models.name: Business State vs. Ticker State
models.oneliner: The price on your screen and the actual health of the company are two different things — most investors only ever look at the first one.
models.full: The umbrella idea under everything else: most investors value the ticker (the price on the screen, which reacts to sentiment, panic and the multiple) when they should value the business state (the roots — margins, ROIC, reinvestment runway, concentration risk, pricing power). His line is that the screener tells you what a business was, and your job is to price what it becomes, because investing is about the future earning profile and guidance, not past data. The link between the two: the multiple follows the business state with a lag — when the roots deepen the re-rating eventually comes, when the roots rot the de-rating comes. To apply it, deliberately separate ‘what is the price doing’ from ‘what is the business doing’ before any valuation call, and inspect the roots directly rather than reacting to the leaf. What’s easy to get wrong is the symmetrical trap: seeing a stock at a now-‘cheap’ multiple and calling it a bargain is the same error as seeing it at 100x and calling it quality — both are staring at the leaf instead of the roots. The discipline is to stop positioning on the ticker/screener number and position on the business state, trusting that price ultimately has no choice but to catch up to whatever the business is actually doing.
models.analogy: Think of a pot with a plant in it. The price tag on the pot doesn't move for months. But underneath the soil, roots can be growing stronger every week, completely invisible until the plant suddenly shoots up. If you only watch the pot's price tag, you'll miss the growth happening out of sight.
models.stockNote: KPIT is the post this model anchors: its roots rotted (European auto R&D cuts, weakening growth) so the leaf fell — and the trap is that people now see it ‘cheap’ and misread the ticker again, the same mistake as seeing it ‘quality’ at 100x. Kovai is the positive mirror: the business state moved enormously (EPS ₹106→₹223, two new verticals, ROCE/ROE 21-23%) while the ticker looked ‘dead’ for two years — there the gap is the opportunity, not a warning. Kalyan made it vivid on results day — the business improved on every vertical (38% growth, 28% same-store) yet the stock cracked 9-10% on optics before rebounding ~25%, i.e. the ticker panicked while the business compounded. Caplin Point is the slow-burn version: cash and capacity strengthened right through the accumulation window (CFO +21%, EBITDA +18%, ANDAs 34→59) while the price sat still, then caught up +57% — price catching up to the business, as it always does.

models.name: The Two-Engine Framework
models.oneliner: Your return = earnings growth × the multiple the market is willing to pay. Both can work for you, against you, or cancel each other out.
models.full: The problem it solves: why two people can buy the exact same stock and get opposite outcomes, and why a company with genuine earnings growth can still lose you money. Every return decomposes into two multiplying engines — the earnings engine (how fast EPS actually grows) and the multiple engine (whether the market pays more or less per rupee of those earnings). The critical link is that the multiple is never random: it follows the business state, re-rating up when margins, runway and ROIC strengthen and compressing when the business weakens. To apply it, split a stock’s past return into the two engines, then — the part most people skip — price the future of each rather than extrapolating the screener: estimate the forward EPS trajectory and ask what multiple that future actually deserves, adjusting for size (a big base can’t grow like a small one). A useful discipline is to ask ‘at today’s price, would I buy this fresh?’ — if no, the thesis needs revisiting even if you’re up. What’s easy to get wrong: valuing the ticker instead of the business state — treating a now-‘cheap’ multiple as a bargain is the same mistake as treating a 100x multiple as proof of quality, both are staring at the leaf (the multiple) instead of the roots (margins, ROIC, reinvestment runway, pricing power). PEG in isolation is a trap for the same reason: it’s computed on past data. The catastrophic case the framework exists to avoid is buying at a peak multiple on peak earnings, so both engines reverse together.
models.analogy: Imagine your paycheck (earnings) multiplied by how confident and generous you feel with money (the multiple). Even if your paycheck goes up 10%, if your confidence craters at the same time, you might still end up spending — and feeling — poorer than before.
models.stockNote: HDFC Bank is the cleanest illustration: EPS grew 188% (₹17→₹49) over ~7 years, yet the stock ‘did nothing’ because the multiple compressed from ~28-30x to ~15x and ate the entire earnings gain — the trigger being a holder’s complaint that six years produced no return. The forward setup flips it: modest 10-12% EPS growth plus a reversion toward 20x as margins repair puts both engines in favour (a 16.5-19% CAGR), so ignoring the framework would have you conclude a sound franchise is broken. KPIT is the mirror image and the worst case the model warns against — bought at a peak 85-100x on peak earnings, so when European auto R&D cuts hit, the multiple and the earnings engine reversed together, producing a 16% crash and a stock that needs a 3x just to break even. Kalyan is the both-engines-favourable pick: ~20-27x with faster growth and multiple room still ahead. Titan is the opposite — earnings moderating and, at 70-80x, no room left in the multiple engine, which is exactly why fresh capital goes to Kalyan. Caplin Point shows the earnings engine compounding at ~21% PAT while he accumulated at only ~15x ex-cash — both engines set to work for him even as depreciation optics mask the earnings strength. And Tata Elxsi shows the multiple engine already fully de-rated (110x in 2022 to ~32x), so from here the two engines can re-align — the ‘window opening’ against KPIT’s value trap.

models.name: The Plateau Framework
models.oneliner: A great business's stock can go sideways for years — not because it's stalling, but because the multiple is quietly compressing exactly as fast as earnings are growing.
models.full: The problem it solves: why a genuinely good business’s stock can go sideways — even drift down — for years, and how to tell that apart from a business that is actually stalling. The mechanism is that a stock’s return has two engines, earnings growth and the multiple the market pays for those earnings, and when they move in opposite directions at a similar pace they cancel out on the ticker. Earnings keep compounding underneath, but the multiple is compressing by roughly the same amount, so the price looks “dead” even as the business quietly gets bigger. To apply it, separate the two engines explicitly over a multi-year window: track the EPS line and the P/E line as two different things rather than just watching price. If EPS is clearly rising while the multiple is falling from an earlier peak, you are on a plateau — the business has moved, the price just hasn’t caught up — and it resolves upward once the multiple compression bottoms out, because from there both engines finally point the same way. The forward test is to project EPS out a couple of years and re-price it at even the current (compressed) multiple; if that already implies a much higher price with zero re-rating, the plateau is doing the work for you. What’s easy to get wrong: reading the flat price action and concluding “nothing is happening” — that is confusing ticker state with business state, when the whole point is that the business state has moved even though the chart hasn’t. The second trap is mistaking a genuine plateau (healthy compounding under a shrinking multiple) for a business whose earnings have actually stopped growing; only checking the underlying fundamentals tells you which one you hold, and the framework only works on the former. As he puts it, bad timing costs you time while bad businesses cost you capital — a plateau is a timing problem on a good business, not a capital-loss problem.
models.analogy: Like water building up behind a dam wall — the surface (price) looks completely calm and unchanging, but pressure (earnings growth) is building the entire time. Once the compression stops, the price has to "release" all at once.
models.stockNote: Kovai Medical is the worked example. The trigger was two years of dead-looking price action against results that kept compounding: EPS went from ~₹106 in FY23 to ₹223 now (more than doubling), yet the P/E sat at 24-25x the whole time — having compressed from a 34-35x peak — so the stock “doubled” off 2023 but went nowhere since 2024-25 purely on multiple compression, not any business weakness. Running the two engines separately produced the conclusion: the business state had moved significantly (two new growth verticals created, ROCE/ROE held at 21-23% without leverage) while the ticker hadn’t caught up, so someone sitting on a 20-25% drawdown from the 2024-25 top was facing a timing problem, not a broken thesis. The concrete payoff: EPS of ₹223 compounding at 16-17% reaches ~₹300 by FY28, which at even an unchanged 24x implies ~₹7,200 with zero re-rating — so the patience is mathematically underwritten. Ignore the model and you would read the flat chart as dead money and sell a compounding business right before the multiple and earnings realign in FY27-28 — exactly the mistake the framework exists to prevent.

models.name: Law of Large Numbers (Size Ceiling)
models.oneliner: The bigger a company already is, the harder it becomes to keep growing at the same fast percentage — because the absolute rupee amount needed gets enormous.
models.full: The problem it solves: knowing when a growth rate is mathematically unsustainable because of size, and why the same multiple carries very different risk at different market caps. The mechanism is simple arithmetic — a ₹100 crore profit growing by ₹30 crore is 30% growth, but once profit is ₹1,000 crore the same ₹30 crore is only 3%. So a 50x PE on a ₹10-20k crore company is a completely different animal from 50x on a ₹1 lakh crore one, because on the larger base the odds are stacked against even generating the growth that multiple assumes. To apply it, always scale the multiple you’re willing to pay to the company’s size: anything near or over ₹1 lakh crore should not command a high growth multiple, because the law of large numbers will drag it back. A second lens is the break-even math — if a large-cap drags 80%, you need a 400% move just to get back, and a high-base EPS engine takes a very long time to deliver that (his examples: Suzlon’s near-two-decade round trip, and the railway/defence names he expects to repeat it). What’s easy to get wrong: paying large-cap prices for the past growth rate on the screener, when that rate is precisely what size makes unrepeatable — the multiple should shrink as the base grows, not stay pinned to history.
models.analogy: It's much easier for a small pond to double in size after one heavy rain than for an entire ocean to double — the ocean needs an almost unimaginable amount of extra water to move the same percentage.
models.stockNote: KPIT is the direct application: at 85-100x on an already-large base, even a healthy absolute profit increase is only a single-digit percentage, so the market compresses it brutally — he walks the arithmetic explicitly (₹30 crore of profit growth is 30% at a ₹100 crore base but just 3% at ₹1,000 crore), which is why paying peak multiples on the larger base guaranteed the down-move once growth normalised. Trent is the same trap at the extreme: ~90-100x on a ~₹3 lakh crore base it reached before retail money piled in, so even a slight EPS slowdown implies a lost decade (an 80% drag needs a 400% recovery). He sizes it against global peers — Zara at ~$130-140B and Uniqlo at ~$100B — to show how stretched Trent looked at a $30-40B cap on that multiple: the runway can’t mathematically justify the price at that size.

models.name: The Caged Bird Model
models.oneliner: A company's "loyal" customers only look loyal because they never had another option — real loyalty is only proven once an alternative shows up.
models.full: The problem it solves: distinguishing a real moat from one that was never actually tested, especially when the bull case leans on long ‘stickiness’ numbers. The mechanism: a bird that never flies away looks devoted, but you cannot measure devotion while the cage door is shut — everything before the door opens is data about the cage, not the bird. So stickiness measured over a period when the customer had no alternative tells you nothing about stickiness once an alternative appears; the day the door opens is the first day loyalty is genuinely being measured (dogs are called loyal precisely because they stay unchained). To apply it, ask whether there was ever a real alternative during the ‘loyal’ years, and only count relationship data observed after a genuine alternative arrives — and note the alternative has to be truly superior on the dimension the customer actually values. What’s easy to get wrong: reading a 15- or 18-year relationship as proof of a durable moat, when it may just be the absence of an alternative, and missing that the environment has changed. His examples travel: ~60 years of Congress dominance before the BJP emerged; kirana stores surviving Big Bazaar and DMart for years but now bypassed by quick commerce (genuinely superior on time and convenience); even long human relationships that dilute once superior alternatives appear.
models.analogy: A bird that never flies away doesn't prove it loves its cage — it just never had an open door. A dog, on the other hand, is genuinely called loyal because it will stay even when it's free to leave. (Author's own analogy — he extends it to 60 years of Congress dominance in India before BJP emerged, and to kirana stores surviving organized retail but not quick commerce.)
models.stockNote: Sagility is the worked example: the bull case leaned on an 18-year average client relationship and 95% stickiness, but those numbers were measured entirely in a pre-AI world where clients had no real alternative to Indian labour-arbitrage — so they measure the cage, not the bird. The door is now opening (AI making the underlying effort cheap), and the tell that loyalty is already being tested is management’s own admission of 150-200 bps of AI-driven cost takeouts in new contracts, rising toward 4-5%. Ignore the model and you’d treat that long stickiness as a durable moat and buy right as the alternative arrives — exactly when the historical loyalty data stops meaning anything.

models.name: The Maginot Line Model
models.oneliner: A moat can be completely real against the old form of competition, and still get made irrelevant when a competitor attacks from a totally different direction.
models.full: The problem it solves: recognising when a moat that is completely real against the old form of competition gets made irrelevant by an attack from a direction it was never built to face. The mechanism is the Maginot Line — France built one of history’s most impressive fortifications, validated by every previous war, and Germany simply went around it through the Ardennes; the moat was never beaten, it was made irrelevant. His business example is BlackBerry: BBM and enterprise security were a genuine moat with corporates locked in, but Apple attacked from a different direction (consumer iOS), so the moat wasn’t breached, it stopped mattering. To apply it, ask which direction the fortress is not facing — a moat built against the old competitor says nothing about a new competitor taking a route it was never designed to block. He pairs it with the Caged Bird as a two-part test: the Caged Bird asks whether the door was ever open (was loyalty ever tested), and the Maginot asks which direction the fortress isn’t facing (can the moat even be aimed at the new threat). What’s easy to get wrong: treating a real, historically-validated moat as protection against all threats, and confusing ‘not breached’ with ‘still relevant.’
models.analogy: France built one of the most fortified defensive lines in history along the German border — validated by WWI experience. Germany just went around it through Belgium's Ardennes forest in WWII. The line was never breached; it just stopped being relevant. Same with BlackBerry: its enterprise security and BBM moat was completely real, but Apple's iPhone attacked from an entirely different angle (consumer experience), and the moat simply stopped mattering.
models.stockNote: Sagility is the application: its client-relationship and stickiness moat was built to defend against other human outsourcing competitors, not against AI making the underlying ‘effort’ it sells worthless — so the threat comes from a direction the fortress was never designed to face, and the moat is bypassed rather than beaten. Run alongside the Caged Bird test (was the loyalty ever tested?), both models point the same way independently, which is what gives him conviction the moat is converting into a liability: you cannot be defended by the very technology whose purpose is to commoditise what you sell.

models.name: The Dealmaker Model
models.oneliner: Every company trades in two markets — the public ticker, and the private "control market" where dealmakers actually buy and sell whole businesses. Follow the private trail before trusting the public story.
models.full: The problem it solves: avoiding IPO, story, and pump-and-dump traps by reading the structure instead of the narrative. It comes from Chris Mayer’s Invest Like a Dealmaker: every business trades in two markets — the public ticker everyone stares at, and the private ‘control’ market where dealmakers and PE firms actually fight over intrinsic value — and the retail investor who only watches the ticker gets blindsided. To apply it, before buying any IPO or hyped story, trace the ownership chain: who owned this privately, at what price, and how fast are they selling it to the public? Is the listing structured as a cash-out (a large offer-for-sale by the promoter)? And where does the ‘fresh’ money actually go — into growth, or round-tripped back to the seller? A second layer is whether the optimism is already priced in: he contrasts Tesla (the world bet against it, so belief turning into execution created the parabolic move) with SpaceX (euphoria already assumes flawless execution, so there’s no disbelief left to convert) — the return you earn even if execution succeeds is a different thing from the risk you carry if it fails. What’s easy to get wrong: letting a ‘cheap’ screener multiple or an influencer’s pitch sell you the story without the structure underneath — the private market has usually already told you the real value, and if insiders are cashing out fast, that is the signal.
models.analogy: Imagine buying a used car from a dealer who bought it from the original owner for $2,000 last month, and is now asking you $10,000 for it. Before paying that, you'd want to know why the original owner sold so cheap, and why the dealer is in such a hurry to flip it back to the public.
models.stockNote: IGI is the full worked chain: Blackstone paid $569.7M for the group in 2023 (~$393M for the India arm), then IPO’d India alone at an implied ~$2.1B — a ~5x mark in 20 months — with a ₹2,750 cr offer-for-sale that is a pure cash-out and ~₹1,324 cr of the ‘fresh’ issue round-tripped straight back to buy Blackstone’s own European arms. Running the lens tells you the listing was engineered as an exit, not to compound for you, which is why he skips it regardless of the headline multiple. Airfloa is the same lens on a smaller SME IPO: the pre-listing rename, the IPO timing, and — the giveaway — proceeds of ~₹91 cr that almost exactly matched the working-capital hole show public money was raised to plug the balance sheet rather than fund growth, while FIIs cut ~97% of their stake into the retail buying. In both, tracing who was selling and where the money went pre-empts the story.

models.name: The Shrinking Host Model
models.oneliner: When a company's fee is attached to an asset whose real value is collapsing, the fee eventually becomes an unbearable cost — and the whole revenue model dies with the asset it depends on.
models.full: The problem it solves: spotting a business whose revenue is a fee feeding on an asset whose value is structurally falling. The mechanism is that the fee is indexed to the wrong variable — a fixed unit like weight or count that never changes — while the market value of the thing being measured collapses, so the fee-to-value ratio explodes. What was cheap ‘insurance’ becomes an unbearable cost, and customers start walking away at the cheapest items first. He calls it a parasite on a shrinking host: comfortable while the host is healthy, but as the host shrinks the bite grows proportionally until both collapse. To apply it, check whether the fee is pinned to a fixed unit or to the actual market value, then run the fee-to-value ratio forward as the underlying price falls, and look for the breakage beginning at the small/cheap end of the range. What’s easy to get wrong: accepting the management framing that ‘lower prices just push more volume, so revenue keeps growing’ — the volume point can be true while the model still dies, because the real issue is the exploding percentage cost, not the unit count. He’s also careful to note the exact per-unit figures are illustrative, so run the real numbers on the specific business.
models.analogy: Like a parasite that feeds on a host organism — comfortable and sustainable while the host is healthy, but as the host shrinks, the parasite's bite becomes proportionally larger and larger, until eventually the host can't support it and both collapse.
models.stockNote: IGI is the worked case: its certification fee is pinned to a stone’s carat weight, not its price. When a 1-carat lab-grown stone was ~$4,000 a ~$40 fee was ~1% of value — cheap, nobody blinked; as that stone falls ~80-90% to ~$400 the flat ~$40 fee becomes ~10% of the transaction, and past a point costs more than the information is worth. The trigger that it’s already happening: below half a carat the fee already runs 3-8% of value and only about half of those stones get certified, versus ~70% overall — the math broke at the small end first and creeps up the carat ladder as prices fall. Ignore the model and you’d accept management’s ‘more stones, revenue still rising’ framing and miss that the fee is indexed to the one variable (weight) that stays fixed while the variable that matters (value) collapses.

models.name: The Pond Theory
models.oneliner: Fragmented, unorganized industries are shallow ponds full of tiny players — when a new technology or scale threshold raises the survival bar, the pond consolidates fast into a few big, trusted "gorillas."
models.full: The problem it solves: reading where an industry is consolidating and, crucially, where a function like ‘trust’ migrates as it does. The mechanism: picture every industry as a pond — the unorganised sector is a vast, shallow pond of millions of tiny players, and when a technology or structural change raises the survival bar, the pond consolidates fast into a few organised ‘gorillas,’ because the minimum size to compete rises exponentially and small players lack the technological and financial firepower to keep up (his examples: quick commerce raising the bar on kirana stores, organised jewellers on the unorganised trade). The key move is that as the market shifts to the gorillas, functions migrate — trust itself moves from an independent third-party verifier to the brand. To apply it, if a business depends on being a trusted middleman, ask whether the gorillas emerging in its industry are about to internalise that function themselves, and position on the future state, not the present one. What’s easy to get wrong: assuming a middleman’s role is permanent, when a strong enough brand can simply become the trust and make the third party optional.
models.analogy: A shallow pond full of countless small fish gets swallowed fast once a few big fish evolve the ability to eat at scale — the small fish don't individually fail, the whole ecosystem just re-sorts around the big players.
models.stockNote: IGI is the application: as the jewellery market consolidates from the unorganised trade to organised gorillas, the trust function is migrating from IGI’s third-party certificate to the retailer’s brand. He points to the shift already visible in IGI’s own concall — Tata’s new lab-grown line (beYon) grades the 4Cs in-house rather than routing through IGI, Tanishq runs in-store verification centres (the De Beers route, where brand plus technology is the assurance), and Kalyan’s leadership tells buyers to ‘believe the brand more than the product.’ Since most Indians trust a Tanishq far more than a slip of paper they’ve never heard of, the day the brand becomes the trust the certificate becomes optional — so allocating to IGI is betting against a structural shift that has already started.

models.name: The Incentive Model
models.oneliner: Before trusting any company's story, ask a blunt question: what is the person or structure in control actually being paid to do?
models.full: His most general-purpose lens (usable on companies, colleagues, careers): strip the narrative and look only at what the person or structure in control is actually incentivised to do, because behaviour follows incentives regardless of what the presentation says. The picture he uses is a landlord about to sell — he doesn’t truly renovate, he does just enough cosmetic work to make the listing photos look good and inflate the price; that is exactly how a PE owner runs a company into an IPO. To apply it, ask blunt questions of the structure: was this built to create value for public shareholders or as an exit for the current owner? Who owns what after listing, how much lock-in is left, how big is the overhang waiting to be sold, and is there any operator with real skin in the game aligned to compounding for you? Then map that answer onto the multiple rather than reading the multiple alone. What’s easy to get wrong: letting a ‘cheap’ screener number or a confident story override the incentive read — if the allocator designed the structure to dump on you, your incentives and theirs are on opposite sides of the table, and no multiple fixes that.
models.analogy: A landlord about to sell a property doesn't truly renovate it — he does just enough cosmetic work to make the listing photos look good and inflate the sale price. That's not fraud, it's just incentives working exactly as designed. (Author's own analogy, applied directly to how PE firms run a company into an IPO.)
models.stockNote: IGI is the closing argument for skipping it: 76.55% still sits with Blackstone (BCP Asia II TopCo) with effectively no lock-in left — a permanent ~77% supply ceiling that will be sold whenever the price recovers — and every structural choice (the round-trip, the near-complete cash-out, loading the loss-making European arm onto retail with their own fresh-issue money) shows the incentive was monetisation, not value creation. Airfloa is the same read on management quality: the incentive was to raise public money and quietly fund a working-capital hole while dressing packaging up as performance, which is why he invokes ‘if you cannot understand the person, don’t do business with them’ — if the capital allocator isn’t honest about the numbers, you preserve your capital rather than partner with them.

models.name: Trap Detection Framework ("Lollapalooza in Reverse")
models.oneliner: Munger's "Lollapalooza effect" is multiple good forces stacking into an outsized win. This is the mirror version — multiple red flags stacking together into an outsized trap.
models.full: Munger’s ‘Lollapalooza effect’ is several good forces stacking into an outsized win; this is the mirror image — several red flags stacking into an outsized trap. The mechanism: individually, a pre-IPO rebrand, a sudden margin jump, negative cash flow, exploding receivables, or a single dominant customer might each be explainable, but when several appear in the same company at the same time they compound rather than cancel, and each additional flag makes the whole pattern more dangerous, not less. To apply it, invert the marketed story and list every red flag you can find, then check whether they cluster and point the same way — a stack of independent warnings is a compounding signal to walk away, and the discipline is to buy moats, pricing power and durable cash flows rather than narratives. What’s easy to get wrong: explaining away each flag in isolation (‘the rebrand is just marketing,’ ‘the margin jump is operating leverage,’ ‘receivables are lumpy’) and being seduced by a hot narrative — in FY24-25 the two easiest themes to raise money around in India were railways and defence, and a company wearing both while failing the cash-flow tests is exactly the pattern to distrust.
models.analogy: Like several small cracks appearing in a dam at different spots at once — any single crack might be survivable, but multiple cracks appearing together usually means the whole structure is about to give way.
models.stockNote: Airfloa is the framework built end to end: the red flags don’t just appear, they stack — a pre-IPO rename (Air Flow Equipments → ‘Airfloa Rail Technology’), an 18-20x profit jump on margins that aren’t structural, negative operating and free cash flow (−₹4 cr and −₹11 cr) despite ₹26 cr of reported profit, debtor days at 242 with ₹127 cr of receivables against ₹192 cr revenue, a monopsony customer (Indian Railways via L1 reverse auctions, so no pricing power or moat), IPO proceeds (~₹91 cr) that just plug a working-capital hole, and FIIs cutting ~97% of their stake while retail buys. Any one might be explained away; all of them together are the Lollapalooza-in-reverse — the compounding warning that the Vande Bharat/defence narrative exists precisely to distract from.

models.name: Percentage-of-Completion (POC) Accounting Trap
models.oneliner: Some companies book revenue today based on their own internal guess of how "complete" a long project is — even before the customer approves it or pays a rupee.
models.full: The problem it solves: catching companies that book revenue today on their own internal guess of how ‘complete’ a long project is — before the customer has approved it or paid a rupee. He breaks it into a four-step loop you’ll see repeat in infra/EPC-style names: (1) shift the revenue mix into turnkey, multi-year contracts; (2) recognise that revenue using percentage-of-completion, i.e. management’s own ‘we’re 70% done’ estimate; (3) front-load the revenue to showcase growth even if the client hasn’t approved the work, no payment has arrived, and delivery is months away; and (4) because the revenue is on paper but the cash isn’t in the bank, receivables explode, the balance sheet bloats, and cash flow turns negative. To apply it, whenever reported profit races ahead, cross-check it against operating and free cash flow and against receivables/debtor days — if profit is up but cash is negative and receivables are ballooning, POC front-loading is the likely mechanism. What’s easy to get wrong: trusting the P&L profit line (an opinion) over the cash flow statement (the fact), and missing that ‘booked’ is not ‘collected.’
models.analogy: A contractor tells you your kitchen renovation is "70% done" and asks to be paid for that 70% today — except you never agreed it was 70% done, and you haven't paid a cent of it yet.
models.stockNote: Airfloa is the four-step loop in the wild: it shifted its revenue mix away from direct Indian Railways work (78%→55%) into turnkey projects (metro, RRTS, exports, defence) recognised on percentage-of-completion, then front-loaded that revenue before approval or payment — which is exactly why receivables exploded to ~₹127 cr against ₹192 cr of revenue (242 debtor days) and free cash flow was −₹11 cr despite ₹26 cr of reported profit. It is the accounting engine underneath the ‘18-20x profit growth’ headline: booked on paper, not collected in cash — so trusting the P&L over the cash flow statement is exactly the mistake the model catches.

models.name: Phoenix Forge & Dragon Flight Framework
models.oneliner: A pre-planned map of price zones for buying more as a stock falls (Phoenix Forge) and adding more as it breaks to new highs (Dragon Flight) — so you're not deciding emotionally in the moment.
models.full: The problem it solves: how to allocate capital methodically instead of emotionally, both as a high-quality stock falls (Phoenix Forge) and as it breaks to new highs (Dragon Flight). The framework pre-sets price zones with sizing for each, but the real work is a single test before any of it: is the falling price a Forge (the business is getting stronger while the price sleeps — a gift) or a Pyre (the business is actually deteriorating — a trap where capital is burned to ash)? The chart never tells you which one you’re holding; only the roots of the business and its environment do (the same fire can burn at the stock, the sector, or the whole-market level). Once confirmed a Forge, you deploy in pre-planned tiers (for example ~20-30% at the first zone, ~50-60% at the highest-conviction middle zone, a small reserve for a black-swan low) so you neither panic-sell nor chase. Dragon Flight is the mirror ladder for adding on the way up, methodically rather than on FOMO, with one level defining which framework is live (above it every dip is a Dragon add; below it the Phoenix reset begins). To apply it well, always align the tier with valuation — if the price hits the next zone but the multiple has run to 100x you slow down and ride rather than add. What’s easy to get wrong: buying just because the PE looks low (a Pyre is cheap for a reason), and trying to time the exact bottom — you never get the perfect entry, which is the whole point of laddering.
models.analogy: Think of stocking up on winter coats before a cold snap you're confident is coming (a Forge) — every price drop is a bargain, because you know demand and value are both about to rise. Buying discounted coats at a store that's actually going out of business (a Pyre) is the opposite: cheap, but for a reason that will burn you.
models.stockNote: Caplin Point is the framework walked band by band. He pre-set Phoenix accumulation zones (Tier 1 ₹1,900-2,050 for 20-30%, Tier 2 ₹1,620-1,830 as the 60% conviction zone, Tier 3 ₹1,350-1,460 for the final 10%), and the stock moved through them almost exactly — ~85 sessions in Tier 1, ~79 in Tier 2, bottoming at ₹1,500 on 30 March without ever reaching Tier 3, then running +57% into a fresh all-time high. The trigger to keep deploying was that fundamentals improved every quarter while the price sat still — a confirmed Forge, not a Pyre. It then flipped to Dragon Flight: he treats ₹1,847 as the level that decides which framework is live (above it every dip is a Dragon add), and the stock breached the ₹2,409 ‘Tier 2’ core window (to ~₹2,450). Ignore the Forge-vs-Pyre test and you might have laddered into a deteriorating business instead — the discipline is what made a falling price a gift here rather than a trap.

models.name: The Depreciation Model / "Hidden Law of Great Compounders"
models.oneliner: When a company is investing heavily in new capacity, the accounting cost hits profit immediately — while the revenue from that investment only shows up years later.
models.full: The problem it solves: why a great compounder can look like it’s slowing down exactly when it’s investing most, and how not to be fooled by it. The mechanism is that depreciation is a non-cash charge that hits the P&L before the revenue from the capex that created it shows up — so when a company front-loads capex, depreciation steps up and compresses reported PAT growth even while the actual cash engine keeps compounding. He frames it as the hidden law of great compounders: they look slow before they look fast. To apply it, whenever a company is mid heavy-capex, read cash flow from operations and EBITDA rather than the bottom-line PAT, and check whether a deceleration in reported profit is really just front-loaded depreciation ahead of the revenue those new facilities will generate. What’s easy to get wrong: seeing PAT growth drop (say from 27% to 21%) and concluding the business is maturing or weakening — most investors run only the PAT line and miss that the company is building for the next decade while still throwing off record cash.
models.analogy: A farmer who just planted a new orchard pays for the digging, planting, and irrigation right now — those costs hit this year's books immediately. But the harvest (the revenue) doesn't arrive for another two or three years. Anyone judging the farm purely on "this year's profit" would wrongly conclude the farm is struggling, right before its best years.
models.stockNote: Caplin Point is the worked case: reported PAT growth ‘decelerated’ from 27% to 21%, which most investors read as maturing — but cash flow from operations grew 21% and EBITDA ~18% over the same period. The cause is front-loaded capex (~₹870 cr over five years, with ~₹500 cr more over 2-3 years on plants still under construction), which pushed depreciation up ~10% YoY and steps it up further as facilities commission through FY27-28 — before the revenue those plants will generate arrives. So the ‘slowdown’ is an accounting artifact ahead of the payoff; ignore the model and you’d sell a compounder mid-investment cycle precisely when it looks slow before it looks fast.

models.name: The Foreshock Model
models.oneliner: A company's first profit warning or growth slowdown is almost never the last one — it's a warning tremor before more come.
models.full: The problem it solves: timing — specifically, when (not whether) to buy a beaten-down ‘quality’ name after a crash. The analogy is literal: earthquakes have foreshocks, and the first tremor is the warning, not the quake. A company’s first guidance cut or growth slowdown is almost never the last, because managements don’t cut once and stabilise — they cut, then cut again as the rot shows up in stages, and like aftershocks the bad news comes fast at first and then decays. To apply it, before buying a dip ask one question: is this the first slowdown, or the Nth? If it’s the first crack, stay out and wait 3-4 quarters for the shaking to settle and a base to form before treating a fallen name as an opportunity — that’s how you shift the odds in your favour. What’s easy to get wrong: buying simply because a stock has dragged 15% and ‘looks cheap,’ which is exactly how the ticker state traps you, since a name can rebound briefly after the first crack and still collapse later. He makes it a default rule: never buy after the first slowdown of any company.
models.analogy: Earthquakes almost always have small foreshocks before the big one — the first tremor is a warning, not the event itself. (This is the author's own direct analogy, used by name.)
models.stockNote: KPIT triggered the model’s clearest statement: after a 16% single-day crash he treated it as a fresh Q1 warning — the first tremor — not a bottom, and refused to catch it, advising a 3-4 quarter wait for the base to form. Trent is the model applied at the other end of the sequence: down 45%, but he counts it as the sixth or seventh slowdown since late 2024, not the first, so it’s still not a buy (and still ~90x). The concrete lesson he draws is that everyone who bought the first crack from ₹5,000 is trapped — proof that buying after the first slowdown, even a big one, is how the ticker state gets you, because more tremors were always coming.

models.name: The Snowball Method
models.oneliner: Add to a position when the business keeps proving new reasons to own it — new customers, a wider moat, stronger execution — never simply because the price moved up or down.
models.full: The problem it solves: when to add to a winner — the exact reader question that prompted it (wait for dips, or buy on strength even at slightly skewed valuations?). The answer reframes ‘snowballing’: it is not adding because the price is going up, it is adding when the business is actually delivering — margins expanding, the moat widening, new reinvestment runways opening, management executing at the same or superior returns on capital. Price moves on noise; the business compounds in silence, so you add on signal strengthening, not on price retreats. Each year of genuine execution should stack another independent reason to own it, until the thesis at Year 10 is unrecognisable from Year 1. To apply it, revisit the thesis and ask whether every variable that mattered when you bought is stronger today; if yes, add regardless of where the price is (a dip is a gift, not a requirement) — and if the price runs up but the variables aren’t strengthening, you might ride or trim, but you don’t deploy fresh capital. What’s easy to get wrong: adding on price momentum, waiting only for dips, or selling on a 50-100% gain just because the ticker moved — the strengthening of the moat and model is the trigger, the price is just the receipt.
models.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill doesn't get bigger because of the shape of the hill — it gets bigger because it keeps picking up new layers of snow. The terrain (price path) barely matters if the snowball keeps collecting real material.
models.stockNote: Symbotic is the model in action: he bought at $14 and added at $24 not because the price dropped but because the business kept proving new layers — the customer list expanded (Walmart-only to Albertsons, Target, Medline and more), Walmart handed over its own micro-fulfillment tech, the cross-facility data flywheel and RPO backlog deepened (~$22B order value, ~$47B economic), and management started solving its own deployment and charging bottlenecks (next-gen storage structure, Nyobolt batteries). Each is an independent reason to add, so he says he’d deploy again even at 2-3x the price if valuations are reasonable. Ignore the model and you’d do the opposite — refuse to add on strength, or sell on an early 50-100% pop — and miss the compounding precisely because the ticker moved before the thesis was done.

models.name: The 100-Bagger Framework (Thomas Phelps)
models.oneliner: The biggest stock winners tend to be small, overlooked companies that meaningfully cut a customer's cost, time, or constraint — with switching costs so high that leaving becomes brutal.
models.full: The problem it solves: identifying the rare setups that can become 100-baggers — and, just as important, whether you have the temperament to hold one. It comes from Thomas Phelps’ ‘100 to 1 in the Stock Market’: the biggest wealth is made in small, unknown, research-minded companies that solve a major problem, held with fortitude. The screen is four forces stacking in one business — the technology reduces the customer’s constraint, reduces their cost, improves their time, and carries a high replacement/switching cost. Three of those transform the customer; the fourth makes leaving brutal, and when all four align the conditions for a 100-bagger are set (his analogues: Mastercard cutting transaction time and friction, and possibly the stablecoin ecosystem). To apply it, test whether a candidate genuinely hits all four forces, then turn the lens on yourself, because Phelps said finding the company is only half the job — the investor needs vision to see the thesis early, courage to hold through short-term noise while the business strengthens, and patience to let it compound. What’s easy to get wrong: finding the right company but not staying with it (selling on a 50-100% gain or on noise), and mistaking one or two of the forces for the full four-force stack — almost everyone finds a winner, almost nobody stays for the full climb.
models.analogy: Author's own comparison: Mastercard became a huge compounder by reducing transaction time and friction for an entire economy — the same four-force pattern he's watching for in payments infrastructure, warehouse robotics, and (he suggests) stablecoins.
models.stockNote: Symbotic is framed explicitly this way: it hits all four Phelps forces — it cuts retailers’ labour cost and delivery time and removes the supply-chain-automation constraint (giving any retailer Amazon-grade efficiency without a 20-year build), and once a ~$500M system plus years of accumulated data are embedded, ripping it out for a cheaper competitor is near-unthinkable (the fourth force that makes leaving brutal). He layers on the Lollapalooza of forcing functions — mandatory adoption to compete with Amazon, plus a structural US labour crisis (40-50% warehouse attrition, wage inflation) — as the tailwind. The framework’s second half applies too: he stresses the vision, courage and patience needed to actually capture it, i.e. not selling the winner early just because the ticker has run.

models.name: Capital Allocator Quality (ROCE vs. ROIIC)
models.oneliner: Debt, cash-hoarding, and pledges aren't automatically good or bad — the real question is whether management is deploying capital in a way that actually creates value.
models.full: The problem it solves: whether debt, a promoter pledge, or cash-hoarding is good or bad — the trigger question being ‘is promoter pledge a red flag?’ His answer: a capital-allocation decision in isolation tells you nothing; you have to ask why it was made and which direction the business moved after. The core tools are ROCE and ROIIC read together — ROCE shows the structural quality of the existing business, ROIIC shows the marginal quality of the new capital being deployed — so leverage is good only when the allocator is good and knows when and how to use it. Add a lifecycle lens: mature compounders self-fund and need no pledge, while a pledge is legitimate earlier when the growth opportunity exceeds internal cash. To apply it, pair ROCE with ROIIC, get inside the allocator’s incentives, and judge which financing tool they picked and why — his worked examples span TransDigm (designed ~5.8x EBITDA leverage funding buybacks and special dividends into a ~27% total-return CAGR), ServiceNow (paying ~$9B for Veza and Armis where year-one ROIIC looks poor but the strategic ROIIC buys longevity and pricing power), Copart (sitting on ~$5B cash yet opening an undrawn multi-currency credit line to borrow in the local currency of each expansion market as a hedge), and Buffett borrowing yen at ~0.5% to collect 3-5% dividends (~6x interest coverage) despite having the cash. What’s easy to get wrong: reading any one variable (pledge, debt, cash) in isolation or screening on the raw number without the structure underneath. His explicit red-flag patterns: capital flowing to the promoter’s personal balance sheet rather than the business, the pledge ratio rising while ROIIC falls, no stated and tracked deleveraging path, and pledged shares sitting at a price where a forced sale triggers a death spiral.
models.analogy: A wealthy person taking a very cheap loan instead of paying cash isn't being reckless if the loan's interest rate is lower than what they'd otherwise earn by keeping that cash invested elsewhere — it's optimization, not desperation. Red flag version: debt or pledges rising while the returns on that capital are actually falling.
models.stockNote: Kalyan Jewellers is the worked Indian example: rather than treating the promoter pledge as an automatic red flag, he reads it as bridge capital at the right point in the lifecycle. The pledge funded store expansion in a category where shelf space and trust compound; the growth is healthy (same-store sales growth alongside new-store additions, not just store-count optics); it’s taking share from the unorganised segment; and the promoters are using operating cash flow to bring the pledge to zero by 2027 on a trajectory you can watch quarter by quarter. Run against his red-flag list — capital going to the promoter’s personal balance sheet, pledge rising while ROIIC falls, no tracked deleveraging path, pledged shares at a death-spiral price — Kalyan clears each, which is why the pledge reads as financing a growth runway that exceeds internal cash rather than distress (he contrasts it with Caplin, which reached scale needing neither debt nor pledge).

models.name: The Linguistic Mental Model
models.oneliner: How a founder or CEO actually talks on earnings calls — the specific words, hedges, and repeated phrases — often reveals what's really happening before the numbers catch up.
models.full: The problem it solves: reading what a founder or CEO actually says on earnings calls to infer what’s really happening before the numbers catch up. The mechanism: every management team has its own linguistic vocabulary, and the words they reach for are a tell — confident operators use concrete numbers and firm timelines, while nervous or promotional managers hide behind vague, hedged adjectives and repeated storytelling. A shift over several quarters from marketing-style language toward blunt, numbers-first commentary is a sign a team has stopped managing perception and started just running the business transparently (and, relatedly, smart allocators tend to under-promise and over-deliver). To apply it, read the language first and then go back to the numbers with that filter on: screen every transcript for operator language versus marketing language, watch how a management’s concall openings change across consecutive quarters, and note ‘temporal honesty’ — an operator repeatedly saying the right things ‘cannot be done overnight’ is describing a slow-turn business truthfully, not making excuses. What’s easy to get wrong: taking management’s framing at face value and being swayed by a good story, when the tone and word choice often reveal more than the polished narrative does.
models.analogy: Like noticing a friend who used to talk about big exciting plans switch to only discussing small, concrete next steps — often a sign they've become more serious and realistic, not less ambitious.
models.stockNote: Kalyan Jewellers is the richest application: on the Q2 FY26 call a BOB Capital analyst pressed promoter Ramesh on COCO stores degrowing 1% despite a gold tailwind, and he named it directly as the deliberate South COCO→FOCO conversion; on the Q3 FY26 call a frustrated retail investor (Srinivas of Phoenix Estate) pushed on the results-vs-price disconnect and Ramesh twice declined to engage, saying it’s ‘not under our control’ — unusually blunt in Indian concall culture, where promoters usually spend half the call managing the share price. He also repeated ‘it cannot be done overnight’ three times across inventory adjustment, 18-karat acceptance and franchisee-margin renegotiation — the same temporal honesty across topics — and tracks a broader shift in the openings across four consecutive quarters from storytelling to numbers-first, all read as honest operator language rather than spin. Caplin Point is the same lens applied to results: he reads the concall tone (confident founders use concrete numbers and timelines) and notes management ‘has never gone for reckless growth,’ flagging a dedicated linguistic decode of Caplin as an upcoming post.

models.name: The Bottleneck Strategy ("Road vs. Toll Booth")
models.oneliner: When a major technology shift happens, find the actual physical choke point all the new activity must pass through — rather than betting on whichever company in the "obvious" category looks best.
models.full: The problem it solves: when a major technology shift happens, finding where the money will actually pool — the real physical choke points every new activity must pass through, not the categories the industry currently sells. The method starts by inverting the core assumption: today’s security stack was built for humans as the actors (slow, accountable, one-per-seat), but AI agents log in thousands of times a minute at machine speed with no HR lifecycle, so the old products become ‘real toll booths sitting on roads that are getting bypassed.’ You then map the brand-new bottlenecks the shift actually creates (here: machine identity, AI runtime inspection, data-access brokerage, unified telemetry, continuous attestation) and ask who sits on each. Two refinements make it sharper. First, watch the private/control market — serious platforms absorb the bottlenecks before retail notices (Alphabet buying Wiz for $32B, Palo Alto buying CyberArk for $25B), so by the time it’s obvious the pure-plays are gone. Second, distinguish a toll booth (captures value from traffic that already exists, so its economics are bounded) from a road (creates the traffic, so its economics expand with everything built on top) — and remember road owners eventually absorb the toll booths through bundling and proximity, the way Bloomberg, AWS, and Visa/Mastercard did. What’s easy to get wrong: betting on the obvious legacy category because it looks dominant today, and confusing a bounded toll booth with the road underneath it.
models.analogy: Instead of betting on which trucking company will dominate a new trade route, buy the company that owns the only bridge every truck has to cross to get there.
models.stockNote: Palo Alto is the public pure-play on machine identity (Bottleneck 1) after the two scaled players were absorbed — CyberArk (which owned category-creator Venafi) into PANW for $25B and Wiz into Alphabet for $32B — a live case of platforms buying the toll booth before it was obvious. CrowdStrike sits on two at once: AI runtime inspection (Charlotte AI watching what agents do after login) and unified telemetry (Falcon Next-Gen SIEM as the data layer other AI security agents plug into), with Microsoft Sentinel the main bundling threat. Rubrik holds the barely-existent continuous-attestation bottleneck: its ransomware-era immutable-backup architecture turns out to be the right base for verifiable rollback of agent actions (Agent Rewind), betting fast reversibility beats perfect prevention. Cloudflare is reframed from toll booth to ‘the road’ — inline by default across three bottlenecks and already the default host for remote MCP servers as Anthropic/OpenAI/Google converge on MCP, so as the road owner it should capture the toll booths built on top. Zscaler sits on runtime inspection too but is his lowest-conviction name, added on community input and openly flagged as not yet ‘placed cleanly’ against SASE-to-AI economics. Varonis was the cleanest data-brokerage specialist (the toll booth moving to the data itself) but was removed mid-post as an ‘anti-Lollapalooza’ — Cyera in private markets, Microsoft Purview bundling, and CrowdStrike/Palo Alto platform absorption all converging against it.
